title: Every Woman Waiting on God Needs This
paragraphs:
Every Woman Waiting on God Needs This
The Waiting You Hate May Be the Place Where God Is Preparing the Miracle You Cannot Yet See
There is a kind of pain almost no one talks about.
It doesn't leave bruises anyone can photograph.
It doesn't announce itself with tears every day.
Sometimes it hides behind a smile at church.
Sometimes it sits quietly at family gatherings while everyone else seems to be moving forward.
Sometimes it whispers at midnight...
"God... did You forget me?"
Maybe you've prayed for a husband.
Maybe you've prayed for healing.
Maybe you've prayed for children.
Maybe you've prayed for reconciliation.
Maybe you've prayed for direction.
Maybe you've prayed for freedom from anxiety.
Maybe you've prayed for a breakthrough that seems delayed far beyond what your heart thought it could endure.
The hardest part isn't always the waiting.
The hardest part is wondering whether Heaven is still listening.
If that is where you are today...
Don't stop reading.
Because this isn't merely another motivational article.
This is about discovering that some of God's greatest works are born inside seasons that feel painfully silent.
Not because He has abandoned you.
But because He is preparing something that your present eyes cannot yet recognize.
The Bible never hides the reality of waiting.
Scripture never pretends that faithful people always received immediate answers.
Instead, it introduces us to women whose waiting became part of God's redemptive story.
Sarah waited decades before Isaac was born.
Hannah wept until her pillow became an altar before Samuel arrived.
Ruth endured loss before experiencing redemption.
Elizabeth carried years of disappointment before giving birth to John the Baptist.
Mary lived through confusion before witnessing the resurrection.
None of these women understood the ending while they were living the middle.
Neither do we.
One of the Hebrew words translated "wait" is קָוָה (qāvâ).
It means far more than simply passing time.
Its original picture carries the idea of being twisted together like strands of a strong rope.
Biblical waiting is not passive.
It is remaining intertwined with God.
Isaiah 40:31 says:
"But they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint."

The phrase "wait for the LORD" comes from קֹוֵי יְהוָה (qōvê YHWH)—those who actively place their hope, confidence, and expectation in the Lord. The promise is not that waiting itself produces strength, but that the Lord renews the strength of those who trust Him.
Notice something astonishing.
God never promises that waiting will be easy.
He promises that He Himself will sustain those who wait on Him.
That changes everything.
Because waiting is no longer empty time.
Waiting becomes sacred ground.
Our culture measures success by speed.
God often measures maturity by faithfulness.
Abraham waited.
Joseph waited.
David waited.
The disciples waited.
Even after Jesus rose from the dead, He instructed His followers:
"Stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high." (Luke 24:49)
Before Pentecost came...
There was waiting.
Before the Church exploded across the world...
There was waiting.
Before miracles...
There was waiting.
Before purpose...
There was waiting.
Perhaps your waiting is not punishment.
Perhaps it is preparation.
Psalm 27:14 says:
"Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD!"

The Hebrew imperative חֲזַק (ḥazaq) means "be strong," while יַאֲמֵץ לִבֶּךָ (ya'amēṣ libbekha) means "let your heart become courageous." Biblical courage is not the absence of fear but choosing to trust God in the presence of it.
Sometimes we imagine that if God loved us, He would remove every delay.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals another pattern.
God often uses delay to deepen dependence.
When Lazarus became sick, Jesus did not rush immediately to Bethany.
John tells us something almost shocking:
"Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer..." (John 11:5–6)
His delay was not a denial of love.
It was the stage upon which God's glory would be displayed.
What felt like abandonment became resurrection.
Could it be that what feels like God's silence in your life is not the absence of His care but the unfolding of His wiser purpose?

The New Testament often uses the Greek word ὑπομονή (hypomonē), usually translated "steadfastness," "endurance," or "patient perseverance." It literally describes remaining under a burden without giving up. It is not passive resignation but active faith that continues to trust God's promises.
James 1:3–4 says:
"For you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing."
Notice the order.
Testing.
Then endurance.
Then maturity.
We usually want maturity without testing.
God lovingly works through both.
Perhaps no woman in Scripture illustrates surrender more beautifully than Mary.
When the angel Gabriel announced that she would bear the Messiah, her future instantly became uncertain. She faced misunderstanding, social shame, and enormous personal cost.
Yet her response was:
"Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word." (Luke 1:38)
The Greek phrase Ἰδοὺ ἡ δούλη Κυρίου (Idou hē doulē Kyriou) means, "Behold, I am the female servant of the Lord." Mary did not understand every detail, but she entrusted herself to the God who did.
Faith is not having every answer.
Faith is trusting the One who does.
If your heart feels weary today, remember that your identity is not found in your relationship status, your age, your career, your disappointments, or the prayers that remain unanswered.
Your identity is found in Christ.

Ephesians 1 repeatedly reminds believers that they are chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, and sealed in Him. These blessings are rooted in God's grace through Christ, not in changing life circumstances.
Jesus Himself knows what waiting feels like.
He waited thirty years before beginning His public ministry.
He waited in Gethsemane while His closest friends slept.
He endured the silence of Saturday before the joy of resurrection morning.
Even on the cross He cried:
"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46)
The Gospel preserves Jesus' words in Aramaic:
אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה שְׁבַקְתַּנִי (ʾĒlī ʾĒlī lamā šəvaqtanī?) according to the Matthean form (closely related to Psalm 22), meaning, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"

Jesus was quoting Psalm 22, a psalm that begins in anguish but ends in confident hope and the proclamation of God's saving work. Even in His suffering, He was fulfilling Scripture and accomplishing our redemption.
Because of His death and resurrection, our waiting is never without hope.
The greatest scandal in history was not merely that humanity rejected the Son of God.
It was that the sinless Savior willingly bore our sin so that guilty sinners could be declared righteous through faith in Him.
The cross looked like defeat.
It became the doorway to eternal victory.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
From scandal...
To grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If He can transform a cross into salvation...
He can transform your waiting into worship.
He can transform your disappointment into deeper dependence.
He can transform your tears into testimony.
He can transform your broken story into a display of His glory.
Maybe today your miracle is not that God immediately changes your circumstances.
Maybe today's miracle is that He changes your heart while you wait.
You never know whether a single act of encouragement may remind a weary heart that God has not forgotten them.

Return to the Scriptures. Read them slowly. Pray them honestly. The God who was faithful to Sarah, Hannah, Ruth, Mary, Elizabeth, and countless saints throughout history has not changed. His timing is perfect, His promises are trustworthy, and His grace is sufficient.
The God who writes redemption has never misplaced a single page of your story.
